lines: Grab a thick steak — an inch or more. Ribeye or strip is the most forgiving; thick means you can't easily overshoot it.
Press paper towels firmly into both sides until nothing more comes off. Boring step, biggest payoff — dry steak is what sears.
Salt both sides — more than feels right — and add pepper if you like. Press it in so it sticks.
Nothing goes on the heat yet — the first step of the cook handles that. Just have your heaviest pan ready; cast iron is the champion.
Get tongs, a resting board, and butter within reach. You'll pull the steak a touch early — it keeps climbing while it rests.
Get tongs, paper towels, and a resting plate next to the grill. You'll pull the steak a touch early — it climbs while it rests.
Heaviest pan on high heat, empty. About two minutes on gas — closer to four on electric. It needs to be screaming hot.
Add a thin layer of oil. Wait until it shimmers.
Lay the steak into the pan, away from you. Now don't touch it.
That sizzle is your crust forming. Leave it alone and let it build.
Time to flip. Lift a corner — if it's deep brown, flip it once.
No rush — another 30 seconds. You want deep golden-brown, not grey. Check again after.
How's the crust? Tap “I flipped it” once it's over.
Beautiful — second side's searing now.
Drop the heat to medium, then add a spoon of butter, plus garlic and thyme if you have them.
Spoon the butter over the top of the steak, again and again.
Stand the steak on its edges with your tongs and sear the fat, about thirty seconds each side.
The solo's kicking in right as you hit the home stretch. Almost there.
Almost there. Keep it steady.
Take the steak onto a board now — pull it about five degrees early, around a hundred and twenty-five.
Aim for about a hundred and twenty-five to a hundred and thirty now — it rises to medium-rare as it rests.
Almost there — pop it back in the hot pan for another 30 to 60 seconds, then check again. You're close.
Check again — tap “It's there” once it's around 125 to 130.
Perfect — now it rests and climbs to medium-rare.
Burner off — then let it rest at least five minutes. Don't cut into it; that's what keeps it juicy.
Spoon the cowboy butter over the rested steak, or serve it alongside.
Rest's done. Slice it against the grain and dig in. You just made a steakhouse steak for about fifteen bucks.
Grill's hot. Give the grates a quick scrape, and get ready to lay the steak over direct heat.
Lay the steak over the hot zone, away from you. Now don't touch it.
Rotate the steak forty-five degrees, same side, for crosshatch marks.
If it flares up, slide it to the cooler side for a moment, then back.
Time to flip. If side one's deeply marked, flip it once.
No rush — another 30 to 60 seconds for deep marks. Slide it off direct heat if it's charring, then flip.
How are the marks? Tap “I flipped it” once it's over.
Nice — second side searing now.
Give it another forty-five-degree turn for marks on this side.
Take the steak off onto a board — pull it about five degrees early, around a hundred and twenty-five.
Almost — back over direct heat for 30 to 60 seconds, then check again. You're close.
Kill the burners — close the valve if you're on gas — and move the steak onto its resting plate.
Get the cowboy butter ready — it goes over the steak once the rest is done, or serve it alongside.

Off the grill and onto the plate — now it rests, five minutes. Drop the butter on top while it waits; it melts right in. Then slice against the grain. You just grilled a steakhouse steak for about fifteen bucks.
Off the grill and onto the plate — now it rests, five minutes. Then slice against the grain. You just grilled a steakhouse steak for about fifteen bucks.
Light the grill. On gas, open the propane valve, turn a burner to high, and press the igniter — check that it lit, then close the lid. It preheats for nine minutes while we prep the steak.
Pat the steak dry with paper towels — press firmly on both sides until nothing more comes off. Dry steak is what sears.
Season both sides with salt — more than feels right — and pepper. Press it in lightly so it sticks.
Get your tongs, a resting plate, and your thermometer next to the grill. If you can, keep one burner lower as an escape zone for flare-ups.
Hold your palm about five inches over the grates. If you have to pull away within two seconds, it's ready. If not, close the lid and give it a few more minutes.
Grill's ready. Grab the steak and your tongs, tap play, and we lay it over direct heat.
Alright — I've got you. Free Bird is rolling, let's cook.
Let's cook. Free Bird is rolling.
Crack your eggs into a bowl — tap each one on a flat surface, not the edge, and you'll get fewer shell bits.
Beat in the milk and salt just until the colour is even — no streaks of white, and don't over-beat.
Set out a nonstick pan, a rubber spatula, and a plate. Your fat goes in the pan later — not the bowl.
Set the heat to medium-high, then add the butter and let it melt.
Pour in the eggs. Now leave them alone — don't stir yet. We're not making rubber.
Let them sit — no stirring. When the edges turn solid white — usually thirty to sixty seconds — tap continue.
Not white yet? Give them a few more seconds on medium-high — still no stirring.
Are the bottom and edges solid white (not runny)? Tap once they've set.
Perfect — now drop the heat and start the figure eight.
Turn the heat down to medium-low, then start the figure eight — trace an eight through the eggs, gentle and steady.
Nice — soft curds are forming. Keep that gentle figure eight going.
Big soft folds, still a little wet — looks underdone, and that's the point. Almost there.
Slide the pan off the burner and turn the burner off. One more gentle fold — the pan's own heat finishes them.
You want fluffy broken curds — pillowy soft pieces with no runny raw egg. Pull them now; they finish off the burner.
No rush — back on low for a few seconds, then check again. No runny raw egg, but keep the curds soft.
How do they look? Tap “Just set” once there's no runny raw egg.
Perfect — fluffy, soft curds.
Season with salt and pepper, plate up, and eat while they're soft. You just made scrambled eggs from scratch — nice work.
Set the heat to medium-high, then add the oil.
Set the heat to medium-high, then coat the pan with spray.
Turn the dial down to medium-low and lift the pan off the coil for twenty to thirty seconds while it cools — then back on, and trace a gentle figure eight.
Put your empty pan on the burner and turn it all the way up to high. Nothing in it yet — no butter, no oil, no eggs. Just let it get hot.
Flick a few drops of water on the pan — it's ready when the drops ball up and dance around like tiny marbles. If they just sit and fizzle, give it another thirty to sixty seconds.
Nice and hot. Tap to start — we bring the heat down to medium-high and add your fat, then the eggs go in.
Alright — I've got you. Here Comes the Sun is rolling, let's cook.
Let's cook. Here Comes the Sun is rolling.
Get everything within reach before the heat goes on — this cook moves once it starts.
Measure out your pasta — the box tells you the weight, and the screen shows exactly how much you need.
Measure out your liquid and have it ready to pour — it goes in fast, right after the garlic.
Smash each clove flat so the skin slips off, then rock your knife through until the pieces are tiny — about the size of a grain of rice.
Grate your parmesan from the block now and set it aside — it goes in off the heat, near the end.
Measure your cream and keep it by the stove — it pours in slowly during the music.
Cut your chicken into bite-size pieces and season them — they cook first, before the butter goes in.
Slide the pot off the burner to a cold spot — don't just turn the dial off; the burner stays hot for minutes. Let it rest while the intro plays.
Slide the pot off the burner — don't just turn the dial off. Let it rest a moment while the music settles in.
Pour in the cream slowly, stirring in lazy circles. Let the ballad set the pace — don't rush, or the sauce breaks.
Pour in the cream slowly, stirring in lazy circles. Don't rush it.
Still off the burner, add the parmesan a handful at a time, stirring constantly until each melts. If it clumps, splash in a little of the warm liquid from the pan and stir hard.
Add the parmesan a handful at a time, stirring until glossy.
Here it is — the rock drop! Taste the sauce right now, and season hard with salt and pepper. Be bold — no second-guessing.
Taste the sauce now, and season hard with salt and pepper. Be bold.
Too thin and watery? Back on low and simmer it uncovered a minute or two — don't add water. Too thick and pasty? Loosen it with a splash more of the reserved chicken broth, a tablespoon at a time.
Tear some fresh basil over the top, then plate it up — twirl it into a warm bowl. The outro's starting. You made it.
Tear basil over the top, then plate it up. You made it.
Put the fork down for a second and look at what you made — creamy, glossy, perfectly seasoned pasta, cooked to Bohemian Rhapsody. You earned it.
Put the fork down and look at what you made. You earned it.
That's the cook. One pan, no delivery fee — go eat.
Too thin and watery? Back on low and simmer it uncovered a minute or two — don't add water. Too thick and pasty? Loosen it with a splash more of the reserved vegetable broth, a tablespoon at a time.
Too thin and watery? Back on low and simmer it uncovered a minute or two — don't add water. Too thick and pasty? Loosen it with a splash more water, a tablespoon at a time.
Crank the heat all the way up and melt the butter — on gas it foams fast, so move on the moment it's foaming. Just the butter for now — no garlic yet.
Now add the garlic. Stir it for thirty to forty-five seconds, just until it smells amazing — then go straight to the liquid, before it browns.
Add the pasta and the broth, give it a stir, and keep it on high.
Keep it on high until big bubbles roll across the whole pot — not just the edges. The pot decides when, not the clock. Stir it now and then.
Once it's boiling hard, drop the heat to medium-low for a gentle simmer. Leave it uncovered, and set the timer for your box's cook time.
Bite a piece — if the pasta's tender and the liquid's cooked down into a glossy sauce, you're ready. If not, give it a couple more minutes.
That's the pasta cooked. Slide the pot off the burner — don't just turn the dial off — and tap play. We finish the sauce to the music.
Add the pasta, the water, and the butter — it melts as it heats. Give it a stir and keep it on high.
Pour in the water and stir in the bouillon until it fully dissolves — one cube for every cup of water, no lumps.
Stir the pasta into the broth, and keep it on high.
Crank the heat all the way up and melt the butter. Electric starts slow — give it a few minutes. It's ready when it's foaming, and it's still just butter — no garlic yet.
First, cook your chicken pieces through — about three to four minutes a side, until there's no pink. Then set them aside; they go back in later with the cream.
Alright — I've got you. Bohemian Rhapsody is rolling, let's cook.
Let's cook. Bohemian Rhapsody is rolling.
Press paper towels firmly into the skin until nothing more comes off — dry skin is what goes crispy.
Season both sides with salt and pepper — add garlic powder and paprika too if you have them.
Wash your hands, the board, and the knife with hot soapy water before you touch anything else — this is the one safety step never to skip.
Get a cast iron or stainless pan out — not nonstick — with a little neutral oil, tongs, and a thermometer if you have one.
The thermometer goes in the thickest part right next to the bone — safe at one sixty-five, best around one seventy-five to one eighty-five.
Lay the thighs skin-side down into the hot oil, away from you — they'll release on their own once the skin is seared.
Leave them alone — I know you want to poke them, but they release on their own once the skin is seared.
That steady sizzle is the skin searing — ease to medium if it's spitting hard, and wash up the raw-chicken board while it works.
Nearly there — the skin's going deep golden. Don't rush the flip.
Spoon most of the hot fat off into a heatproof mug first — then lift one, and if it's deep golden and releases freely, flip it away from you.
If it's sticking, the skin isn't seared yet. Leave it another minute — it releases on its own when it's ready.
How's the skin? Tap “Crisp — flipped” once it's deep golden and lets go freely.
Beautiful. Now cook it through on the second side.
Skin up now — five to seven more minutes, taking these bone-in thighs up toward one seventy-five to one eighty-five so they're tender.
Check the thickest part next to the bone — one sixty-five is the safety floor, but these thighs are best at one seventy-five to one eighty-five.
Not yet — give it another minute or two and check near the bone again. Don't rush this one; it has to clear the safety floor.
Check again — tap “Up to temp — done” once the thickest part by the bone is at temperature with no pink.
Perfect — burner off next, then they rest.
Turn the burner off and slide the pan away, then move the thighs to a plate — skin up.
Rest them five minutes — the hardest part of the cook is doing nothing while the juices settle back in.
Not long enough yet? Good instinct — the juices need the full five minutes to settle back in.
Five minutes up? No thermometer earlier? Cut in by the bone now — no pink and clear juices means serve; still pink means back on medium for two to three minutes.
Perfect — crisp skin, juicy meat. You're done.
Serve them up — crispy chicken thighs, cooked by you, for about five bucks when the fried-chicken app wanted twenty-five. First of many.
Put your cast iron or stainless pan on high heat, then add a thin film of neutral oil to coat the base.
Tilt the pan — when the oil thins out and shimmers like water, it's ready. Smoking means too hot, so take it off the heat for a beat.
Pan's ready. Grab the thighs, tap play, and we lay them skin-side down into the hot oil.
Lay the thighs skin-side down over the direct high heat, away from you, and leave them to sear.
Flames licking up? Slide the thighs to the indirect side for a moment until they settle, then back.
Once the skin's deep golden and releases freely, move the thighs to the indirect side, skin up, and close the lid.
Sticking or still pale? Give it another minute over direct — but if you're past seven minutes, move it to indirect anyway before the skin chars.
Deep golden and releasing? Tap “Moved — lid down” once they're over on the indirect side.
Lid down — now it finishes gently over indirect heat.
Lid closed, cook them through on the indirect side, ten to twelve minutes. Every peek dumps the heat — I know you want to look, but don't.
Probe the thickest part next to the bone — one sixty-five is the safety floor, but these thighs are best at one seventy-five to one eighty-five.
Not yet — back to the indirect side, lid down, a few more minutes, then check near the bone again. Don't rush this one.
Perfect — pull them to a plate to rest.
Pull the thighs onto a plate, skin up, and turn the burners down.
Rest them five minutes — the hardest five of the cook, while the juices settle back in.
Five minutes up? No thermometer earlier? Cut in by the bone now — no pink and clear juices means serve; still pink means back over indirect, lid down, two to three minutes.
Serve them up — grilled crispy thighs, cooked by you, for about five bucks when the chicken place wanted twenty-five. First of many.
Light the grill and set up two zones — one side high, the other side off. Close the lid; it preheats about twelve minutes while we prep the thighs.
Pat the thighs dry with paper towels — press firmly into the skin until nothing more comes off.
Season both sides with salt and pepper, add garlic powder and paprika if you have them, then wash up after the raw chicken.
Once it's hot, wipe the direct-zone grates with an oiled paper towel using tongs — that's the anti-stick for the skin. Keep tongs, a plate, and a thermometer at the grill.
Hold your palm about five inches over the direct zone. If you have to pull away within two seconds, it's ready. If not, close the lid and give it a few more minutes.
Grill's ready. Grab the thighs and your tongs, tap play, and we lay them skin-side down over the direct heat.
Alright — I've got you. Let's cook.
Let's cook.
This one gets smoky, and that smoke is the crust forming. Turn your fan on and crack a window before you start.
Divide the beef into four equal golf-ball-sized pieces and roll them loosely — don't pack them tight. Then put them back in the fridge; cold beef makes a juicier burger.

Fold a square of paper towel into a small pad — that's your smash shield. A flattened sandwich bag works too, or just press with the bottom of a small pot. It keeps the beef off the spatula, not off the pan.
Slice or shred your toppings now, and mix the sauce if you want one — mayo and a little yellow mustard. Once the pan's hot there's no time to chop.
Butter the buns and toast them face-down in the pan over medium until golden, then set them aside. Buns first — the burger won't wait for the bun.
Lay everything out within arm's reach: spatula, your smash pads, unwrapped cheese, dressed buns, foil. Beef stays in the fridge till the last second.

Two cold balls into the pan, a few inches apart. Paper-towel pad on top, then smash straight down with your spatula — hard. Thinner than feels right, wider than the bun. Hold the press for ten seconds and keep your face back.
Peel the pad off slowly, season the tops well with salt and pepper — and then leave them completely alone. The pan is doing the work now.
See the edges going lacy and crispy? That's the crust building. Don't flip yet — let it keep searing.
Get the spatula flat and low, forty-five degrees into the pan, and scrape hard under the patty — all of that brown crust belongs to the burger, not the pan. Then flip it in one motion.
Still tearing or sticking? Give it another thirty seconds — the crust comes off clean when it's ready, not before.
That's the crust. Cheese on, fast — side two's quick.
Cheese on one patty the second it lands, then stack the other patty right on top of the cheese. Side two only needs thirty seconds — then slide the whole stack onto its bun.
Cheese not melty? Ten more seconds — the patty heat does it.
That's the move — keep the rhythm going.
Round two. Next cold balls in, pad on, smash hard, hold ten seconds, peel and season. You know the drill now — that's the whole skill.
Same as before — wait for those lacy brown edges, hands off until you see them.
Thirty more seconds. The crust decides, not the clock.
Scrape, flip, cheese, stack — bring it home.
Scrape and flip the last one, cheese, stack, thirty seconds, and slide it onto its bun. Burner off next.
Turn the burner off and slide the pan off the heat — cast iron stays hot for minutes. Every burger's on its bun now.

Here's the smash burger secret — the patties are so thin they cook through by the time the crust forms. If you're ever unsure, peek inside one: juicy, not wet and pink. Cheese melted means you're there.
Middle looks wet? Turn the burner back to high, give the pan thirty seconds, then back in for twenty seconds a side — thin patties recover fast.
Build it while it's hot.

Build it — sauce on the bottom bun, pickles and lettuce, patty stack, top bun. And no resting: unlike your steak, this one gets worse by the minute. A smash burger this good costs about three bucks — the burger app wanted eighteen. First of many.
Put your empty, dry pan on high heat. No oil, no butter — the beef needs to grip the bare pan to build its crust. Let it get seriously hot.

Careful — this pan is hotter than anything you've cooked on. Flick a couple of water drops in: if they hiss, skate, and vanish almost instantly, it's ready. If they sit and bubble, give it another minute.
Pan's ripping. Grab the cold beef balls, tap start, and we smash the first round.
One cold ball into the pan. Paper-towel pad on top, then smash straight down — hard. Thinner than feels right, wider than the bun. Hold it ten seconds and keep your face back.
Cheese on the second it's flipped. Side two only needs thirty seconds — then slide it straight onto its bun.
Divide the beef into two equal pieces and roll them loosely into balls — don't pack them tight. Then back in the fridge; cold beef makes a juicier burger.
Alright — I've got you. Hotel California is rolling, let's cook.
Let's cook. Hotel California is rolling.
Cold day-old rice fries up light and separate. If yours is cold, just break up the clumps with your fingers.
Cut the chicken into small half-inch cubes — smaller than you think — so it cooks fast and evenly.
Crack two eggs into a small bowl and beat them with a fork until the yolk and white are one colour.
Mince the garlic, slice the green onions, and measure the soy sauce so it's all ready to pour.
Line everything up within arm's reach — fried rice cooks fast, so you won't have time to hunt for things once the pan's hot.
Add the chicken and spread it out flat in one layer — then hands off. Let it sit and brown for about ninety seconds.
Give it a first stir and flip the pieces. If the down sides are golden brown, that's exactly right — that's flavor.
Stir every forty-five seconds or so, and cook until no pink shows on the outside — about three more minutes. Add a pinch of salt and pepper.
Time to check the chicken's cooked through. Cut into the biggest piece — it should be white all the way, with no pink.
Still pink inside? Give it another minute or two and check the biggest piece again — chicken's the one thing worth being sure about.
Perfect — scoop it onto a plate and set it aside. It comes back in at the end. Leave the oil and browned bits in the pan.
Add the frozen peas and carrots straight into the hot pan, plus the green onions if you're using them, and stir for about a minute until they're hot.
Add the garlic and stir for about thirty seconds, just until you can smell it — don't let it brown.
Push everything to one side, pour the beaten eggs into the empty side, and stir them gently until they're just set — soft, not dry.
Still wet and runny? A few more gentle stirs — they set fast, so don't walk away.
Add the rice and the chicken back in, break up any clumps, and stir everything together until it's evenly mixed and hot.
Drizzle the soy sauce evenly over everything, add the sesame oil if you're using it, and toss the rice for about two minutes so it all soaks up the sauce.

Taste a spoonful — if it needs more, add a splash of soy. Serve it hot, with sriracha on the side if you like a little heat. That's a full takeout dinner you just made for a couple of bucks. Nice work.
Add a tablespoon of oil to the pan over medium-high heat, and give it a moment until it shimmers and flows easily.
Tilt the pan — if the oil shimmers and flows easily like thin water, it's ready. If it still looks flat and thick, give it another twenty to thirty seconds.
Oil's hot and shimmering. Tap to start — the chicken goes straight in.
Warm your tortillas first — soft ones need twenty to thirty seconds a side in a dry pan, hard shells crisp in a hot oven, then cover with a towel.
Grab your taco seasoning packet — that's your whole spice step. Told you it was easy.
Shred the lettuce, chop the tomato and onion, and grate the cheese if it isn't pre-shredded. Only prep what you're using.
Line it all up by the stove — beef, oil, seasoning, tomato paste, a cup of water for the simmer, your warm shells, and the toppings. Then you're ready.
Add the ground beef and break it into small crumbles with your spatula. Cook, stirring now and then, until it goes from red to brown.
Time to check the beef's cooked through. Cut into a bigger piece — it should be browned all the way, with no pink or red left.
Still some pink? Keep breaking it up and cooking another minute or two — ground beef needs to be cooked all the way through.
Cooked through. If there's a pool of grease, tip most of it out next — leave a little for flavor.

If there's a pool of grease, slide the pan off the heat and carefully tip most of it out into an old can — hold the beef back with your spatula. Leave a little for flavor, and skip it if your beef was lean.
Sprinkle the taco seasoning over the beef and stir for about a minute, until every bit is coated and you can smell the spices.
Stir in the tomato paste if you're using it, then add about half a cup of water and stir it into a loose, saucy filling.
Drop the heat to medium-low and let it bubble gently for three to four minutes, until the liquid cooks down and the meat is juicy and lightly saucy — not dry, not watery.
Still watery? Give it another minute uncovered. Gone dry? Splash in a little more water — the meat should look glossy and moist.
That's it — turn the burner off and slide the pan off the heat; a coil stays hot for minutes and would keep drying the meat. Now build while it's warm.
Spoon the meat into your warm shells, then pile on the cheese, lettuce, tomato, and onion — whatever you're using. This is the fun part.
Grab one, add hot sauce or a squeeze of lime if you've got it, and dig in while everything's warm. That's taco night for about three bucks a head — the taco truck wanted thirteen. First of many.
Add a tablespoon of oil to the pan over medium-high heat, and give it a moment until it shimmers.
Oil's hot and shimmering. Tap to start — the beef goes straight in.
Add your spice blend over the beef and stir for about a minute, until every bit is coated and you can smell the spices.
Mix your spices in a small bowl — chili powder, cumin, paprika, garlic powder, oregano, and a pinch of salt and pepper. That's your packet, from scratch.
Whisk the flour, baking powder, sugar and a pinch of salt together in a big bowl — about ten seconds, so the baking powder spreads evenly. Baking powder, not soda.
Crack the egg into the same bowl and pour in the milk — and the vanilla too, if you're using it.
Whisk just until the dry flour disappears — twenty to thirty seconds. Small lumps are good; they cook out. Don't overmix, or the pancakes turn out flat.
Get your station ready — pan on the stove, butter and a paper towel within reach, your quarter-cup measure sitting in the batter, and a plate for the stack.
Scoop a quarter cup of batter and pour it into the middle of the pan. It spreads itself. Now leave it alone.
Bubbles will start rising to the surface over the next couple of minutes. That's the pancake talking to you, so no poking yet. But if you smell it browning, don't wait — flip it early.
When bubbles cover the whole surface and the edges look dry, slide the spatula all the way under and flip it from the wrist — one smooth motion.
Bubbles only at the edges and the middle still glossy? Give it twenty to thirty more seconds — the bubbles will spread to the middle when it's ready.
Bubbles across the whole top yet? Tap Flipped it once it's turned.
Golden underneath? That's exactly it. Second side is faster — under a minute.
The second side only needs thirty to sixty seconds. Lift the edge to peek — golden means done. Onto the plate and cover it.
How did number one come out? Golden and fluffy means you've got the rhythm. Pale means let the pan reheat a bit. Too dark means drop the heat a notch.
First pancake's always the test-drive — nobody's is pretty. Pale? Pan's too cool, wait longer before the next pour. Too dark? Drop the heat a notch. The rest of the stack inherits the fix.
Golden both sides, fluffy middle? If not, nudge the heat, then tap Got the rhythm.
Locked in — from here it's just reps.

Now it's reps — and quicker than the first, now the pan's dialed in. Pour, wait for the bubbles, flip, out. Fresh butter every couple of pancakes, keep the stack covered. When the batter's gone, cut the heat and pull the pan off it — that's the last thing.
Burner off, if it isn't already. Stack them up, butter on top, syrup over the edge. That's a twelve dollar diner stack for about a buck fifty — and yours is fresher. Nice work.
Set the pan to medium and melt a little butter — then wipe most of it off with a paper towel. That wipe is what saves your first pancake.
Flick a drop of batter on the pan. A gentle, steady sizzle means it's ready. Nothing means wait. Violent spatter means it's too hot, so pull the pan off and back the dial down.
First one's the lesson — the rest are just reps. Tap to pour your first pancake.

Sort out your rice first — the bowl needs two cups cooked, which is one microwave pouch or about three quarters of a cup dry. If you're cooking it fresh, get the pot going now, it takes about fifteen minutes.

Cut the chicken — about half a pound, one breast — into even bite-size cubes so they cook at the same speed. A pinch of pepper is all you need; skip the salt, the soy sauce brings plenty. Wash your hands and board after.

Whisk the sauce in one small bowl — soy, brown sugar, a couple tablespoons of water and cornstarch, plus the vinegar, ginger and garlic if you're using them. Whisk until the cornstarch fully disappears; lumps now mean a lumpy glaze later.
Get the broccoli on deck — florets in a microwave-safe bowl with a splash of water and a lid or plate on top. Don't start it yet; the cook tells you exactly when.
Stage everything by the stove — chicken, the sauce bowl, oil and your spatula all within arm's reach. The glaze phase moves fast, so you want it all set before the pan gets hot.
Add the chicken and spread it flat in one layer. Leave it about ninety seconds before the first stir — that contact time is where the golden edges come from.
Start the broccoli in the microwave now — five minutes, covered. It finishes right as the chicken does, and that's the whole trick. The pan stays your focus.
First stir — if you see golden sides, that's perfect. Now keep it moving, a stir every forty-five seconds or so, until no pink shows on the outside.
Slide the pan off the heat, then cut the biggest cube open. White all the way through with no pink means it's done — a hundred and sixty-five degrees if you're using a thermometer.
Still pink in the middle? Back on the heat a minute or two, then check the biggest cube again — chicken's the one thing worth being sure about.
Cut the biggest cube — white all through? Tap when there's no pink.
Cooked through — slide it back on and drop to medium, the sauce is next.
Give the sauce one last whisk, pour it all in, and stir constantly — it thickens fast, don't walk away.

When it's shiny, thickened, and coating every piece — and your spatula leaves a trail across the pan — that's the glaze. Slide the pan off the heat right away; the dial alone isn't enough. If it's gone gluey, a splash of water off the heat brings it back.

Still watery? Keep stirring on medium — it turns fast, under two minutes, and the shine is the signal. Gone gluey and clumpy instead? Slide it off the heat, stir in a splash of water, and it comes right back.
